passages.t: Those who plot to seize fields
passages.happening:
“Woe to those who devise iniquity and plot evil on their beds!” (verse 1). At morning light they carry it out, ‘because the power is in their hands’ (verse 1). ‘They covet fields and seize them; they take away houses. They deprive a man of his home, a fellow man of his inheritance’ (verse 2).

So the LORD says he is planning a disaster against this nation from which they cannot free their necks, and they will not walk proudly any more (verse 3). People will mock them with a bitter song: their fields have been handed to traitors (verse 4). They will have no one in the assembly of the LORD to divide the land by lot (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The eighth century brought wealth from trade and royal administration to a class of officials and landowners, while small farmers, open to drought, taxes and war, fell into debt. When debts could not be paid, fields and houses were seized, and families could lose their land for good. Micah, from a country town, may have seen it with his own eyes.

In Israel's law, land was not an ordinary thing to buy and sell. Each tribe, clan and family had received its portion when Israel entered the land, and the land belonged to God. A family's field was its inheritance, its living and its place among God's people. The law provided for land to return to its family in the Year of Jubilee, and it forbade moving a neighbor's boundary stone. Naboth refused to sell his vineyard to King Ahab because it was his fathers' inheritance.

The punishment fits the crime. The rich plan evil on their beds; God plans disaster against them, with the same verb. They seized fields; their own fields will be divided. When God restores his people, they will have no share in the dividing of the land.
passages.later: The law says of the land, ‘it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me’ (Leviticus 25:23). Isaiah pronounced woe on those ‘who add house to house and join field to field’ (Isaiah 5:8), and Naboth refused to sell his fathers' inheritance (1 Kings 21:3).
passages.hard:
Were the land-grabbers breaking any law, or only taking advantage of a legal system?

Micah's charge may cover both. Some seizures were probably plain fraud or violence, but many may have been technically legal, through foreclosure on debts or bought courts; Micah later says judges took bribes. Micah's point is that legality is not the measure. God's law aimed to keep every family on its inheritance, and the laws of Jubilee and redemption were designed to prevent a family losing its land for ever. Using legal means to defeat the law's purpose is still injustice in God's eyes.

Interpreters differ on how directly these laws should shape modern economics. The principle is clear: power must not be used to strip the vulnerable of their living. The book's standard is God's covenant, not any modern program or party.
passages.asks: They lay awake planning how to take what was not theirs. Ask what you lie awake thinking about. And ask whether anything you have was gained in a way that was legal but not right.

passages.happening:
The people tell Micah not to preach. He should not preach such things, they say; disgrace will not overtake them (verse 6). Should the house of Jacob say that the Spirit of the LORD is impatient? Do God's words not do good to the one who walks uprightly (verse 7)?

But lately God's people have risen up like an enemy. They strip the robes off unsuspecting travelers (verse 8). They drive the women of God's people from their pleasant homes, and take God's gift from their children for ever (verse 9). So they must get up and go, for this is no place of rest (verse 10). If a man of wind came and lied, promising to preach about wine and beer, “he would be just the preacher for this people!” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Verses 6 to 11 are an argument. Micah quotes the people's words and answers them. The word for preach literally means to drip, perhaps for words falling like rain, or used mockingly for dribbling speech, and it comes five times. The people want the prophets to stop. They are sure disgrace will not come.

God answers that his words do good to the upright. It is not his word that is the problem but their lives. The robes stripped from travelers recall the law that a poor man's cloak taken as a pledge must be returned by nightfall. The women and children driven from their homes were the most vulnerable, often widows and orphans, whom the law commanded Israel to protect.

The preacher they would welcome is a man of wind. The word is ruach, which means wind and also spirit: a windbag, with no Spirit in him, promising wine and beer.
passages.later: The law said, ‘You must not mistreat any widow or orphan’ (Exodus 22:22). Isaiah heard the same demand from his hearers, who wanted the prophets to speak ‘pleasant words; prophesy illusions’ (Isaiah 30:10).
passages.asks: The people wanted a preacher who promised good times. Ask whether you prefer teachers who tell you what you want to hear. And ask who in your world is being driven out of their home, and whether anyone is speaking for them.

passages.t: The remnant gathered, and the King goes before them
passages.happening:
‘I will surely gather all of you, O Jacob; I will collect the remnant of Israel’ (verse 12). God will bring them together like sheep in a pen, like a flock in its pasture, a noisy crowd.

‘One who breaks open the way will go up before them; they will break through the gate, and go out by it. Their King will pass through before them, the LORD as their leader’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends suddenly, turning from judgment to hope without warning, a pattern that comes again in the book. The God who scattered will gather.

The picture is of a shepherd who brings his flock together, and then of a leader who breaks open the way. The one who breaks through goes first, and the people follow him out through the gate. Their King goes before them, and the King is the LORD himself.

The remnant is a theme that runs through Micah: those who are left after judgment, whom God gathers and leads (4:7; 5:7-8; 7:18).
passages.later: Isaiah also pictures the LORD as a shepherd: ‘He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms’ (Isaiah 40:11). Ezekiel heard God promise to gather his scattered sheep (Ezekiel 34:12-13).
passages.asks: The LORD goes first through the gate, and his people follow. Ask where God has gone ahead of you into a place you feared. And ask what it would mean for you to let him lead you out.
